COrAL: Order-Agnostic Language Modeling for Efficient Iterative Refinement

Yuxi Xie, Anirudh Goyal, Xiaobao Wu, Xunjian Yin, Xiao Xu, Min-Yen Kan, Liangming Pan, William Yang Wang

Paper ↗Code ↗

COrAL lets a language model predict and revise several token positions within a local window, making the trade-off between reasoning accuracy and decoding speed explicit.

01 / The research question

Why should a token become permanent as soon as it is generated?

Ordinary autoregressive decoding commits to an output from left to right. A later phrase can make an earlier choice look wrong, but the decoder does not revise that choice in place. Asking the model to critique and regenerate its answer creates another sequential pass. Parallel decoding addresses latency, yet independently proposed tokens can also disagree with one another. COrAL studies these two problems together: how to keep the useful sequential structure while making nearby predictions revisable.

The important restriction is local. Learning arbitrary orderings over an entire sequence is difficult; COrAL instead learns dependencies within a bounded window. A target position may be predicted from an earlier prefix or reconstructed with some later text available. These are different views of the same position, and their agreement can help decide what to keep.

03 / Inside the method

Train for revision, then decode with several views of each position

The training objective has two complementary parts. Forward training predicts several future positions from clean sequences. Reconstruction training corrupts patches of a sequence and asks the model to recover the original tokens, with loss applied to corrupted positions. Patch replacement and repetition create errors that the model must learn to repair. Refinement is therefore a trained capability, rather than an instruction added to an unchanged next-token model.

Predicting different positions from one context also requires knowing which position is being queried. COrAL modifies RoPE in the final attention layer so that the query is encoded for the target position. This target-aware representation avoids a separate output head for every offset. Training is staged: adapt the last layer first, then train the network more broadly, reducing the mismatch with the pretrained model.

At inference, a sliding block contains positions to predict or revise. The model combines available conditional distributions, with weights reflecting dependency distance and context confidence. It constructs candidate blocks and verifies them using next-token and backward probabilities, with an additional contrastive term. An acceptance procedure determines how much of the block's prefix can be committed. Only that accepted prefix moves the window forward; the remaining positions can be reconsidered.

  1. 01

    Learn local dependencies

    Train for forward prediction and backward reconstruction within a limited context window.

  2. 02

    Decode in blocks

    Predict and revise multiple positions as a sliding block advances through the response.

  3. 03

    Choose a refinement budget

    Adjust verification and parallel prediction to trade computational cost against answer quality.

04 / Reading the evidence

Accuracy and speed change with the decoding setting

  • +4.6 pp

    GSM8K · accuracy setting

    Accuracy rises from 74.1% to 78.7% without multi-forward prediction; this setting runs more slowly than the baseline.

  • 3.9×

    GSM8K · speed setting

    Removing verification increases throughput, while accuracy falls to 72.4%. The largest speed and accuracy gains use different settings.

The ablations separate two contributions. On GSM8K, the full system raises accuracy from 74.1% to 75.3% while increasing accepted-token throughput from 39.7 to 43.4 tokens/s. Removing multi-forward prediction keeps backward refinement and reaches 78.7%, but throughput falls to 14.9 tokens/s. Removing verification reaches 156.8 tokens/s, while accuracy falls to 72.4%. The 4.6-point gain and 3.9× speedup describe different operating points.

The code results expose a boundary that the headline numbers miss. HumanEval pass@1 drops from 64.6% to 13.0% with the full method, and the paper's error analysis identifies syntax as a major failure source. Disabling multi-forward prediction recovers 61.6%, at lower throughput. Local agreement is useful for refinement, but it is not enough to ensure globally well-formed programs. The experiment asks where flexible token ordering helps, and where stronger structural constraints are needed.

Scope. Parallel refinement is sensitive to output structure: the full method performs poorly on HumanEval, so the reported reasoning gains do not generalize to code generation. Read the study ↗

Research summary

Iterative refinement has emerged as an effective paradigm for enhancing the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) on complex tasks. However, existing approaches typically implement iterative refinement at the application or prompting level, relying on autoregressive (AR) modeling. The sequential token generation in AR models can lead to high inference latency. To overcome these challenges, we propose Context-Wise Order-Agnostic Language Modeling (COrAL), which incorporates iterative refinement directly into the LLM architecture while maintaining computational efficiency. Our approach models multiple token dependencies within manageable context windows, enabling the model to perform iterative refinement internally during the generation process. Leveraging the order-agnostic nature of COrAL, we introduce sliding blockwise order-agnostic decoding, which performs multi-token forward prediction and backward reconstruction within context windows. This allows the model to iteratively refine its outputs in parallel in the sliding block, effectively capturing diverse dependencies without the high inference cost of sequential generation. Empirical evaluations on reasoning tasks demonstrate that COrAL improves performance and inference speed, respectively, achieving absolute accuracy gains of 4.6% on GSM8K and 4.0% on LogiQA, along with inference speedups of up to 3.9× over next-token baselines. Preliminary results on code generation indicate a drop in pass rates due to inconsistencies in order-agnostic outputs, highlighting the inherent quality–speed trade-off. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/YuxiXie/COrAL.
